# Attribute resolution and schema classes

Four classes come from the step where the runtime builds a node's attribute
bag, checks it against the executor's declared schema, and — after the
executor returns — checks what the executor wrote back. No executor is
involved in raising them; the runtime raises them itself.

None of the four carries an emitter prefix. They are bare words:
`template_resolution_failed`, `template_validation_failed`,
`executor_schema_unavailable`, `attributes_schema_failed`. Write them into
`error_types` exactly as spelled — see [routing.md](routing.md) for why a
prefix pattern will not reach them.

All four are ordinary policy-routed classes: an `error_types` entry naming one
of them acts on it, and the four actions all apply.

---

## `template_resolution_failed`

**What produced it.** The runtime could not resolve a substitution directive
into a value while filling the node's attribute bag — the directive names a
source that is not there. It is also the class the runtime uses as its
catch-all for any attribute-resolution failure it cannot classify more
precisely, and the class raised when a claim's lock-spec substitution fails
during acquisition.

**What else you get.** A `template_resolution_failed` event lands on the node
before the policy runs, carrying `directive` (the substitution directive that
failed), `site` (where in the node it appeared), `field` and `reason`. Read
that event first: it names the exact directive.

**Can `error_types` act on it.** Yes. `retry` rarely helps — the directive
will still be unresolvable next attempt unless an upstream node is expected to
publish the missing value.

**What to change.** Fix the directive in the template. Either the referenced
node, claim, param, message or env var does not exist, or it exists and has
published nothing by the time this node dispatches. If the source is an
upstream node, check that this node subscribes to it.

---

## `template_validation_failed`

**What produced it.** The resolved attribute bag failed validation against the
executor's declared attributes schema at dispatch, before the executor was
called.

**What else you get.** A `template_validation_failed` event with the same
`directive` / `site` / `field` / `reason` payload shape.

**Can `error_types` act on it.** Yes, but a retry re-runs the same resolution
against the same schema and fails identically. Route it to `give_up` or `pass`
according to whether the node's failure should stop downstream work.

**What to change.** Fix the node's `attributes` block so the bag it produces
satisfies the executor's schema. `POST /v1/templates/validate` catches most of
this at registration time — but it needs a live deployment, because the answer
depends on which executors that deployment has.

---

## `executor_schema_unavailable`

**What produced it.** At dispatch the executor named by the node had no
visible declared attributes schema. Either the executor's capabilities
handshake had not completed, or the discovery cache held nothing for it.

**Can `error_types` act on it.** Yes, and this is the one of the four where
`retry` is the right answer. The condition is transient: it clears as soon as
the executor's handshake lands. Pair `{action: retry}` with a
`retry_backoff` and a `max_retries` cap so a permanently absent executor still
terminates.

**What to change.** Nothing in the template, usually. Check that the executor
service is running and reachable, and that it answers its capabilities RPC
with a non-empty `expectedAttributesSchema`. `GET
/v1/observability/executors/{name}` shows what the deployment currently sees.

---

## `attributes_schema_failed`

**What produced it.** The executor completed successfully and returned an
attributes delta, and the merged bag failed the node's schema at commit. The
run does not settle as a success: the delta is rejected and the failure routes
through `error_types` instead.

**What else you get.** An `attributes_schema_failed` event carrying the
validation message.

**Can `error_types` act on it.** Yes. Note the sequencing: the executor
already did its work. A `retry` re-invokes the executor from the start.

**What to change.** Either the node's `attributes.schema` is stricter than
what the executor actually writes, or the executor is writing a shape it
should not. The event's message names the offending field.
